Despite discrimination, the promise of jobs compelled the Chinese to stay. They mined in Gold Canyon and settled along the Carson River in this area. 39.23613,-119.58936: Dayton. Dayton, one of the earliest settlements in Nevada, was first known as a stopping place on the river for California–bound pioneers. Called by several different names in its early years, the place became Dayton in 1861, named in honor of John Day who laid out the town.For many decades Dayton prospered as a mill and trading center. It remained the county seat for Lyon County until 1911.
39.23614,-119.59064: Union Hotel & Post Office. The original Union Hotel was located across the street. It was rebuilt here in 1870 after a fire destroyed the old hotel. 39.23679,-119.92879: The Great Incline Of The Sierra Nevada. Located on the mountain above are the remnants of the “Great Incline of the Sierra Nevada”. 39.23792,-119.59248: Dayton School House 1865. In 1865 Lyon County built this imposing stone school building for the residents of Dayton, then the county seat. 39.23809,-119.59112: Courthouse Site 1865 1909. Dayton was the first seat of Lyon County and had one of the first courthouses built in Nevada. Utilizing the ruins, the Nevada legislature funded the construction of a high school that opened in 1918. The school closed in 1959 and the building became an elementary school, then a junior high school and is now the Dayton Valley Community Center.
39.23875,-119.59125: Camels In Dayton. Camels were imported into the United States for military purposes in the mid-1850’s. Lt. Used extensively between Sacramento and Nevada points for some ten years, they were later abandoned to fend for themselves. Few were seen after the 1880s.
39.26455,-119.63958: Silver City School House. The growing town of Silver City built a schoolhouse at this site in 1867-1868. Enrollment was as high as 166 students during the 1880s. 39.26662,-119.6432: Devil’s Gate. It gives ... “a forcible impression of the unhallowed character of the place.” J. 39.2714,-119.84079: Franktown. 39.2722,-119.56817: Sutro. Sutro was a town, a tunnel, and a man. The well-planned community was headquarters for the Sutro Drainage Tunnel.German-born Adolph Sutro came to the Comstock in 1860. 39.28469,-119.84061: Bowers Mansion. BUILT— 1864 RESTORED —1967 Bowers Mansion recalls the wealth of the Comstock Bonanza. 39.29882,-119.65566: Mc Cone’s Foundries. In 1862, Ivy Mead, John McCone and Mr. Tascar established a foundry at Johntown, two miles southeast of here in Gold Canyon. 39.30194,-119.65113: Chollar Mine. First located in 1859, the Chollar was consolidated with the Potosi in 1865. As the Chollar-Potosi, it was one of the leading producers on the Comstock. 39.30535,-119.651: Savage Mansion (C. 1861). 39.30665,-119.6502: Mackay Mansion. Once the residence of John Mackay, this elegant mansion also served as the office for the Gould & Curry Mining Company. 39.30811,-119.82499: The Winters Ranch Rancho Del Sierra. This large Gothic-style structure, completed about 1864, was the ranch home of Theodore and Maggie Winters and their seven children. 39.3101,-119.6497: Mark Twain. 100 years ago, in 1864, Samuel Clemens left the territorial enterprise, moving on to California and worldwide fame. He was a reporter here in 1863 when he first used the name, Mark Twain. He later described his colorful adventures in Nevada in “Roughing It.”
39.31053,-119.65096: The Great Fire Of 1875. The most spectacular calamity to befall Virginia City had its origins within fifty feet of this marker. 39.31054,-119.64838: African Americans And The Boston Saloon. Between 1866 and 1875, a remarkable business thrived directly behind this building. Free-born William A.G. 39.31099,-119.65011: Piper’s Opera House. This building, the most significant vintage theatre in the West, was erected by John Piper in 1885. 39.31305,-119.8974: Mount Rose Weather Observatory. Two miles to the northwest of this point lies Mt. Rose. 39.31617,-119.64727: The Comstock Lode. Near this spot was the heart of the Comstock Lode, the fabulous 2 ½ mile deposit of high-grade ore that produced nearly $400,000.00 in silver and gold. 39.3527,-119.86029: Galena Creek Fish Hatchery. The Galena Fish Hatchery represents an attempt to make amends after Nevada’s Comstock Lode ravaged the region’s ecosystem in the 1860s and 1870s. 39.36256,-119.81753: Galena. Galena began as an important lumbering center and mining camp. In 1860, R. S. and Andrew Hatch laid out the town and organized a mining district. 39.37575,-119.71593: Geiger Station. 39.37996,-119.74232: Steamboat Springs. These natural hot-springs are notable for their curative reputation. They were acclaimed by President Ulysses S. 39.44134,-119.77187: Huffaker’s. Before the arrival, 1858, of Granville W. Huffaker driving 500 head of cattle into the Truckee Meadows, the principal settlers were Mormons. 39.47598,-119.75415: Emigrant Donner Camp. 39.48897,-119.79482: Junction House. One of the busiest crossroads of pioneer Nevada converged at this point, serving many major toll roads of the area. 39.49112,-119.80001: Moana Springs. Opened as a resort on October 29, 1905, Moana Springs took its name from a famous Hawaiian spa.
